narrative: Fire and drought interactions dominate today's climate-linked findings: a six-month camera-trap study in Namibian savanna shows mammal occupancy declining progressively in burned areas while small carnivores and burrow-associated species suffer the steepest losses, and a global-change study finds that weak before-after experimental designs systematically underestimate drought impacts on river ecosystems. Movement and behaviour research highlights indirect pathways of ecological influence, from spotted-tailed quolls and Tasmanian devils acting as secondary dispersers of mycorrhizal fungal spores through mycophagous prey, to free-ranging lizards actively regulating UV exposure independent of thermoregulation. In plant-herbivore and invasion ecology, UV-B and silicon jointly shape cereal anti-herbivore defence allocation, reduced litter allelochemicals are shown to facilitate invasional meltdown among alien species, and a common garden experiment across Europe finds invasive knotweed relies on phenotypic plasticity rather than local adaptation. Landscape and conservation studies range from regenerating forestry clearcuts acting as ecological traps for woodland caribou, to sediment supply being identified as the key lever for sustainable waterbird conservation in the Yellow River Delta. On the methods front, a review of 7,356 conservation-evidence studies documents a decades-long shift toward more robust before-after-control-impact and randomised designs, alongside new tools for automated dry-stone-wall mapping from airborne laser scanning and an evolutionary algorithm for lighter bioacoustic classifiers.
